# Problem 1

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
data("ny_noaa")
view(ny_noaa)
```

`ny_noaa` has `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables (`r paste(names(ny_noaa))`). 

Exploratory analyses (describing some key variables, and indicating the extent to which missing data is an issue):

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(across(id:tmin, ~mean(is.na(.x))) * 100)
```

Missing data are an issue in this dataset. 43.7% of maximum and minimum temperature observations are missing. Snow depth is missing 14.7% and precipitation is missing 5.6%. There are no missing values for ID or date.

### Do some data cleaning. Create separate variables for year, month, and day. Ensure observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall are given in reasonable units. For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?

```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date)
  )

ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

ny_noaa |> 
  count(snow) |> 
  arrange(desc(n))
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 which makes sense because days with no snow all report the same value, whereas days with snow have different measurements in mm so days with one specific measurement are less common than a day with 0 mm.

## Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?

```{r}
plot_maxtemp =
  ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (*C)"
  )

plot_maxtemp
```

Average maximum temperatures are consistently higher in July than in January across all weather stations and years. There is no obvious consistent increasing or decreasing trend over the study period. A few potential outliers are visible, particularly a station with an unusually low average maximum temperature of approximately 14°C in July around 1988 and another with a January average below −13°C in the early 1980s. These outliers could reflect unusual weather conditions, geographic differences between stations, or incomplete observations.

### Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.


```{r}
plot_temp =
  ny_noaa |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )

plot_temp

plot_snow =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  )

plot_snow

plot_temp + plot_snow
```

# Problem 2

Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables; exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data; and encode data with reasonable variable classes (i.e. not numeric, and using factors with the ordering of tables and plots in mind).

```{r}
nhanes_covar = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  ) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

nhanes_df =
  left_join(nhanes_covar, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")
```

### Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, education) |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

nhanes_df |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, education, age) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  )
```

Participants with less than a high school education tend to be older, with median ages around 60–61 years for both men and women. Participants with a high school equivalent education have more variation in age between sexes, with a median age of approximately 53 years for men and 62 years for women. Participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger, with median ages of approximately 44 years for men and 41 years for women. Overall, participants with higher education levels tend to be younger, and the largest difference in median age between men and women is observed in the high school equivalent category.


### Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.


```{r}
nhanes_total =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, age, sex, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with increasing age across all three education categories, although there is considerable variability between participants. Among participants with less than a high school education, men and women have relatively similar activity levels, with a particularly steep decline after approximately age 60. Among participants with a high school equivalent education, women tend to have higher total daily activity than men between approximately ages 30 and 55, but activity levels become more similar at older ages. Among participants with more than a high school education, women generally have higher activity levels than men, although both groups show declining activity with age. There is also a notable outlier in this group, with a male participant around age 35 having almost no recorded activity.

### Accelerometer data allows the inspection activity over the course of the day. Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. Describe in words any patterns or conclusions you can make based on this graph; including smooth trends may help identify differences.

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 361, 721, 1081, 1440),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM", "12 AM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Across all three education levels, average activity is lowest overnight, increases sharply in the early morning, remains relatively high throughout the day, and declines in the evening. Participants with less than a high school education appear to have the highest peak activity levels, particularly in the morning, while those with a high school equivalent education generally have lower daytime activity levels. Women tend to have higher daytime activity than men across all three education categories, although the difference is most pronounced among participants with more than a high school education. In this group, women have consistently higher average activity throughout much of the day, while men and women have more similar activity levels overnight. Overall, the general daily activity patterns are similar across education levels, but the magnitude of activity and differences between sexes vary.

# Problem 3

### Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset.

```{r}
citibike_012020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  ) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

citibike_012024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

citibike_072020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

citibike_072024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    citibike_012020,
    citibike_012024,
    citibike_072020,
    citibike_072024
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )
```

`citibike_df` contains `r nrow(citibike_df)` observations and `r ncol(citibike_df)` variables (`r paste(names(citibike_df), collapse = ", ")`). Each observation represents an individual Citi Bike ride in January or July of 2020 or 2024. The dataset contains a 1% sample of rides lasting less than four hours.

The variables include ride ID (`ride_id`), bike type (`rideable_type`), day of the week (`weekdays`), ride duration in minutes (`duration`), starting and ending station names (`start_station_name` and `end_station_name`), membership status (`member_casual`), year, and month.

The datasets were combined using `bind_rows()`, and year and month variables were added to identify when each ride occurred. Month, weekday, membership status, and bike type were converted to factors, with month and weekday ordered chronologically.


### Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.


```{r}
citibike_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
  )
```

The number of Citi Bike rides increased substantially from 2020 to 2024 for both casual riders and members. Members accounted for the majority of rides in all four months, although casual rides also increased considerably. In both years, the number of rides was much higher in July than in January, likely reflecting warmer weather and more favorable biking conditions. July 2024 had the highest number of rides (47,156), while January 2020 had the lowest (12,420).

### Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Five Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```

### Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.

```{r}
plot_citibike_median =
  citibike_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = factor(year),
    group = factor(year)
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Citi Bike Ride Duration by Day, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

plot_citibike_median
```

Median Citi Bike ride duration was consistently higher in July than in January and in 2020 compared to 2024 across all days of the week. In both years and months, median ride duration was generally longer on weekends. Median ride durations in January 2024 were relatively consistent throughout the week. Overall, these patterns may reflect greater recreational bike use during warmer months and on weekends, while the shorter durations in 2024 could suggest changes in how Citi Bikes are being used over time.

### There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration in 2024 by Month, Membership Status, and Bike Type",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  )
```

In 2024, casual riders generally had longer ride durations than members, particularly for classic bikes. Among casual riders, classic bikes had higher median ride durations than electric bikes in both January and July. In contrast, members had relatively similar ride durations across bike types in January, while electric bikes had slightly longer median ride durations than classic bikes in July. Across all groups, the distributions were right-skewed, with most rides being relatively short but some lasting more than 200 minutes.
